:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Here, $C$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix and $D$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix. 

There are $3$ columns in $C$ and $3$ rows in $D,$ so $C$ and $D$ are conformable for multiplication:

$$
\underset{\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} \times \color{green}{\fbox{3}}}{C} \underset{\color{green}\checkmark}{\cdot} \underset{{\color{green}\fbox{3}} \times \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2}}{D} = 
	\underset{\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} \times \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2}}{CD}
$$

Let's compute $CD,$ one element at a time:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{bmatrix}, &  & \,-4=1\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot 2+0\cdot (-3) \\  & \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ ∗ & ∗\end{bmatrix}, &  & \,1=1\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 0+0\cdot 2 \\  & \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ -1 & ∗\end{bmatrix}, &  & \,-1=2\cdot 0+1\cdot 2+1\cdot (-3) \\  & \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}, &  & \,4=2\cdot 1+1\cdot 0+1\cdot 2\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Multiplying Two Matrices When They Are Conformable

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Let $C=AB.$ What is the value of $c_{32}$, if
![](images/c6/c6c7e580cfd96bc23c55742535ceb40a94635c2a44b911e0d08311c3a599c2fa.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Multiplying the $3$rd row in $A$ by the $2$nd column in $B$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{32} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 4 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot 4+2\cdot (-2) \\  & =4-4 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding an Entry of the Product of Two Matrices

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Here, the first factor is a $3 \times 1$ matrix and the second factor is a $1 \times 2$ matrix. 

There is $1$ column in the first matrix and $1$ row in the second matrix, so the product is well defined:

$$
\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} \times {\color{green}\fbox{1}} {\color{green}\checkmark} {\color{green}\fbox{1}} \times \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} = 
	\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} \times \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2}
$$

Computing the product, we have

$$
\eqalign {
    \left\lbrack
    \matrix {
       -1 \
 	0 \
        -2
    }
    \right\rbrack

    \left\lbrack
    \matrix {
        2 & -5
    }
    \right\rbrack

	&= 

    \left\lbrack
    \matrix {
        (-1)\cdot 2 & (-1)\cdot (-5) \
        0\cdot 2 & 0\cdot (-5)\
        (-2)\cdot 2 & (-2)\cdot (-5)
    }
    \right\rbrack \[5pt]

	&=

    \left\lbrack
    \matrix {
       -2 & 5 \
       0 &  0 \
       -4 &  10 
    }
    \right\rbrack 
}
$$
